## The idea

The lowest sounding pitch changes how the notes above it are understood. A root
on every downbeat makes a progression easy to identify, though the result can
soon feel predetermined. A bass line acquires direction when it treats those
roots as destinations and connects them with chord tones, passing tones, and
*approach notes*, pitches a semitone above or below the next target.

Begin with the unadorned roots because they provide an audible reference. If
that version does not state the progression clearly, extra motion will disguise
the harmonic fault rather than solve it. Once the roots work, preserve their
downbeat arrivals and change the route between them. The comparison then tells
you what the connective notes contribute.

Rhythm helps the bass become a line rather than the bottom member of a chord.
It might sustain a downbeat, walk in quarter notes, or anticipate the next root
off the beat. What gives the part independence is that its pattern responds to
the harmony without copying every duration of the melody.

## Run this

The progression moves through C, A minor, F, and G. The first pass exposes its
four roots, one to a bar. The walking version fills each bar with quarter notes:
root, fifth, a directional passing tone, and a chromatic approach from below to
the next downbeat.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :fm

roots = [note(:c2), note(:a1), note(:f1), note(:g1)]

define :play_root_bass do |root_notes|
  root_notes.each do |root|
    play root, release: 3.6, amp: 0.7
    sleep 4
  end
end

define :play_walking_bass do |root_notes|
  root_notes.each_with_index do |root, index|
    next_root = root_notes[(index + 1) % root_notes.length]
    fifth = root + 7
    passing = root + (next_root > root ? 4 : -3)
    approach = next_root - 1

    [root, fifth, passing, approach].each do |pitch|
      play pitch, release: 0.75, amp: 0.7
      sleep 1
    end
  end
end

play_root_bass roots
sleep 2
play_walking_bass roots
```

The long roots in the first statement act as four harmonic pillars. In the
second, those pillars remain on the downbeats, but the bass is already leaning
toward the next one by beat 4. Listen especially to the semitone between each
approach note and the following root. That small distance makes the arrival
sound intended rather than arbitrary.

## Change one thing

1. Make `approach` equal `next_root + 1`. Each chromatic note now falls into its
   target from above. Compare the direction before all four roots; one formula
   need not produce equally convincing voice leading at every boundary.
2. Restore the approach and change `fifth` to `root + 12`. The octave reinforces
   the root but supplies less harmonic contrast than the fifth. Listen for a
   wider line whose second beat repeats identity instead of adding a new chord
   tone.
3. Zip the four pitches with durations `[1.5, 0.5, 1, 1]`. The bar still totals
   four beats, but the held opening root and quick second event change the
   line's gait. Compare that rhythm against a melody of steady quarter notes.

## Why it works

Downbeat roots define the sequence because low register gives them unusual
perceptual weight. Notes between those roots can be unstable for a moment if
the structural targets arrive clearly and on time. A chromatic approach lies
outside the current chord, yet its half-step resolution immediately explains
why it was there.

Passing tones need a route. When two roots are a third apart, a scale step can
fill the space with obvious direction. Across a larger interval, chord tones on
strong beats make the path easier to hear, while less stable pitches tend to
work better in metrically weaker positions. These are interacting constraints,
not a table of universally permitted notes: the next root, current chord,
meter, and melodic register all shape the choice.

The code keeps the four roots as source data and calculates connective notes in
one function. That leaves the root-only bass available as a regression test.
If the walking version arrives on a different downbeat, examine its indexing
and duration sum before replacing individual pitches. The harmony may be
correct while the timeline is not.

Low register also changes timbre. A piano pitch that remains distinct can turn
to undifferentiated rumble on an FM or sub-bass synth because its partials
accumulate differently through speakers and headphones. Try raising the entire
line an octave before reducing amplitude. The problem may be spectral density,
and volume alone will leave that density intact.

## Take it further

Choose an eight-bar progression from an earlier harmony lesson. Render one root
per bar, then derive a walking line that reaches those same roots on every
downbeat. Include at least four chromatic approaches and four diatonic passing
tones, identifying each in comments so its purpose can be reviewed. Give the
walking line a rhythm distinct from the melody and validate each bar's total.
Play root and walking versions in sequence, listening for whether the added
motion clarifies the route between chords without weakening their arrivals.
